name: Theodore Roosevelt National Park
author: parks-page-legacy
summary: Theodore Roosevelt National Park in the badlands of western North Dakota memorializes the 26th president and the landscape that profoundly influenced his conservation philosophy. Roosevelt first came to the Dakota Territory in 1883 to hunt bison and subsequently established two cattle ranches — the Maltese Cross and Elkhorn — in the Little Missouri River badlands. His experiences with the harsh beauty of the landscape and his witness to the decimation of wildlife and open range shaped his lifelong commitment to conservation. As president from 1901 to 1909, Roosevelt established the United States Forest Service, created 5 national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 bird reserves, and 150 national forests, protecting roughly 230 million acres. The park was designated a national memorial park in 1947 and redesignated a national park in 1978.
